item.title: Comment on o1 pro by David Khoo
item.description:
Having used these high-end models extensively as part of my job, I find their problem is precisely how they give answers that sound smart to whoever is asking. You *should* find that suspicious. They agree with you. They make you feel clever. They don't argue violently, flat out disagree, attack your assumptions and arguments, and generally behave like actual human interlocutors unless you press them very unnaturally. I've read the logs that Tyler has posted of "good economic reasoning" by o1, and from the questions you can see that the model is being nudged toward the conclusions that Tyler finds smart. These models act as mirrors, or even yes-men. That's how their RLHF and system prompts make them. That's why they sound so smart to whoever uses them. Yes, they also give you some factual information, but good old search engines or Wikipedia are better sources of these.

It's also why I find conversing with them usually a waste of time. It's amazing initially. Then you realize you're learning very little from what you're reading. I'd rather read smart people I disagree with. I don't want to read smart sounding arguments. I'd rather read arguments from someone like even Krugman that sound stupid at first, then make me think harder and wonder if I'm the stupid one, or we're both stupid.

Part of this is the unclear identity of LLMs. When I talk with a person, there is some relationship between us, that lets me model the other person's mind and contextualize what's being said. I have some idea what their assumptions and motives are, what the consequences of their speech or my speech may be. If a person agrees with me, it makes a difference if they are a friend being nice, or an opponent grudgingly conceding, or a professional giving paid advice, or a salesman trying to sell me something. But with an LLM, it's a void, or a shapeshifter. Contextualization is impossible.

item.title: Comment on Sundry observations on the Trump tariffs by Massimo
item.description:
Tariffs are ugly, but they will be phased out one day. What will remain is the enormous loss of reputation of the US, already decimated by the spiteful utterances about Greenland and Panama. Most people believe that the US is extremely powerful, but all that power has historically been used mostly for good.

This perception is shattering. Nobody can trust the US in this moment. The damage to humanity will be epochal, and I am afraid it will start pretty soon with proliferation of nuclear weapons. The post-war agreement that developed countries were not supposed to develop nukes in exchange for the US umbrella is over. I fully expect not only countries like Germany or Japan developing nuclear weapons, but also mid-tier nations under potential threat, like Poland, Finland, Korea or Taiwan.
